title: The knower of dream and waking
theme: Knowing as the great, all-pervading self that by which one sees both the dream state and the waking state, the wise one does not grieve.

words.role: verb of the relative clause; subject people at large

sandhi.rule: Final m → anusvāra before a consonant, P. 8.3.23 (मोऽनुस्वारः).
The ru of -aḥ becomes u before a voiced consonant, P. 6.1.114 (हशि च), and a + u → o, P. 6.1.87 (आद्गुणः).

samasa.meaning: the ‘end’ (state, sphere) of dream; Śaṅkara takes anta as ‘middle’

morphology.note: Present of dṛś (suppletive stem paśya-) with anu: ‘see along, see throughout’.
Accusative singular of mahat; the strong stem mahānt- has the long vowel.

translation.literal: ‘Having understood as the great, all-pervading self that by which one perceives both the state of dream and the state of waking, the wise one does not grieve.’
translation.readable: ‘The one by which we see both our dreams and our waking days — knowing that as the great self that pervades all, the wise do not grieve.’

anvaya: स्वप्नान्तम् जागरितान्तम् च उभौ येन [लोकः] अनुपश्यति, [तम्] महान्तम् विभुम् आत्मानम् मत्वा धीरः न शोचति ॥
syntax: A relative clause (yena anupaśyati, objects svapnāntaṃ jāgaritāntaṃ ca ubhau) whose correlative is supplied — Raṅgarāmānuja: ‘tam is to be supplied with mahāntam’, «महान्तम् इत्यत्र तम् इति शेषः». The main clause has the absolutive matvā with a double accusative (ātmānam, qualified by mahāntaṃ vibhum).

ambiguities.note: Śaṅkara: by the self, «येन आत्मना अनुपश्यति लोकः», to be known as ‘I am the Supreme Self’, «साक्षादहमस्मि परमात्मेति». Raṅgarāmānuja: by the Supreme Self, which has taken the role of the mind and senses, «इन्द्रियभावमापन्नेन येन परमात्मना».

metre.name: anuṣṭubh
metre.note: Two half-lines of 16 syllables, four pādas of eight.

beginner: Every night we dream and every morning we wake. The dream world and the waking world are very different, yet the same 'I' is there in both, noticing each. This verse points to that witness. Śaṅkara says the Upaniṣad repeats the teaching of the previous verse because it is so subtle and easy to miss: just as one knower knows all colours and sounds, one knower sees both dreaming and waking. When a wise person understands this knower as the great self that pervades everything, grief loses its hold, because what grieves is always tied to one state or another, and this is not. The second line repeats, word for word, the end of an earlier verse (1.2.22), where the self was described as bodiless among bodies.
analogy: A cinema screen that carries a comedy in the afternoon and a tragedy in the evening, and is wet with neither the rain nor the tears.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: That by which one sees both dreaming and waking — knowing it as the great, all-pervading self, the wise do not grieve.

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Śaṅkara: because the self is very subtle and hard to know, the same point is made again, «अतिसूक्ष्मत्वाद्दुर्विज्ञेयमिति मत्वैतमेवार्थं पुनः पुनराह»; the rest is as in the previous verse, «सर्वं पूर्ववत्». The understanding meant is direct: ‘I am the Supreme Self’, «साक्षादहमस्मि परमात्मेति».

commentary.q: Raṅgarāmānuja: the Supreme within the senses
commentary.label: comparative
commentary.text: The one by whom people see the whole dream world and waking world is the Supreme Self, which has become, as it were, the mind and senses, «इन्द्रियभावमापन्नेन येन परमात्मना»; the second line he leaves as already explained, «उक्तोऽर्थः».

commentary.label: linguistic
commentary.text: The second line, mahāntaṃ vibhum ātmānaṃ matvā dhīro na śocati, is the second line of 1.2.22.

advaita.text: The witness of dream and waking is the self; knowing it directly as ‘I am the Supreme Self’, «साक्षादहमस्मि परमात्मेति», the wise one does not grieve.

visistadvaita.text: The one by whom the world sees in both states is the Supreme Self acting through the senses, «इन्द्रियभावमापन्नेन येन परमात्मना».

schools.disagreement: For Śaṅkara the witness is one’s own self, identical with the Supreme; for Raṅgarāmānuja it is the Supreme as the inner ground of the senses, distinct from the seeing self. In our source Madhva’s comment filed with 2.1.4–5 concerns 2.1.5 only.

parallels.quote: महान्तं विभुमात्मानं मत्वा धीरो न शोचति

parallels.note: The person moving between the two ‘ends’, dream and waking, like a great fish between two banks.

contemporary.text: Moods and states come and go — dreaming, waking, good days and bad. The verse suggests that grief loosens when one notices what is present through all of them. (A modern reflection.)

reflect.beginner: In your last vivid dream, who was having it?
reflect.deeper: Why should knowing the witness of dream and waking end grief?
reflect.practice: On waking tomorrow, before getting up, notice what was there both in the dream and now.

flags.note: ‘That by which one sees’ is the self for Śaṅkara and the Supreme within the senses for Raṅgarāmānuja.
